translation.en: [uncertain: Cococe]t of the letter to the wife of the Councillor of War Mr. v. Triebenfeld, née Reichts, has for a long time pained me as much as Your otherwise esteemed communication of the 20th of last month, which I received yesterday; for from it I was to perceive that it were impossible for the same to cast a suspicion upon the manner of conduct I have observed toward you, which nevertheless man be nothing other than good and befitting our friendly relations, and never at any time has been otherwise. May this sincere expression of my feeling serve Your etc. as a convincing proof, should such still be needed toward you, how how firmly grounded my high respect and friendship toward you are, and how much I wish that the same might regard from the single correct side that which I shall have the honour of promising you in what follows. I perceive very plainly from Your etc. communication that the same do not regard at all the measures I have taken concerning the Aslips of Your Rthlr

so as I wished and desired this for your reassurance, on which account I find it necessary to set out the particulars to you most clearly. It was, namely, in the past January of the year 1807 that the Justes Eysach from Berlin arrived here, and [came] to arrange with me a debt outstanding from earlier times. As much as this incommoded me, I nevertheless had grounds which determined me to employ every possible means in order to satisfy this man as to his demand. This took place through the mediation of the Privy Councillor Major, whose old acquaintance Eysenhardt is, and with sacrifices on my part which pained me infinitely. It happened several weeks later that I had received from Your the known instruction for 6000 Rthl from [uncertain: Stettinius], and since the said Eysenhardt entered into the above-noted arrangement under

no other condition than that, if I urgently needed the money from him, I should pay him the [uncertain: Kienier] of 1500 Rthl in cash against his demand; I therefore seized without further ado the expedient of ceding to him the cession from me, and indeed even from Privy Councillor Meyer, the Alligl. held by Your, upon the condition that he pay out to me the remainder of 3,500 Rthl, that is: after the collection of the whole 6000 Rthl, in cash. This I did all the less scrupulously since, as Your can easily satisfy yourself, at that time I could not know the least thing of the suspension of payment arranged by the same. I therefore [expected] quite calmly to receive my money from Mr. Eys. in due course, when from him I first received the most highly

unexpected news that they had suspended the payment that was to be made. My embarrassment was thereby - I confess it to Your - increased in more than one respect, inasmuch as I partly stood in most urgent need of the expected 3,500 Rthl, but partly also had to foresee that sooner or later I should have to pay the 2,500 Rthl [owing] to Eys. by some other means. Nevertheless I also took the requisite steps at Breslau, in order, according to Your p wish, likewise to suspend the disbursement of the 6,000 Rthl. This is the true course of this affair up to the present point in time, and I have, and He [has] to justify me most fully, now only to add this further, namely what I have done in this matter with regard to your wishes. When, namely, I received your communication of the ——, in which the same desired the [uncertain: Zweck Gabe] of the oft-mentioned Alligl., I resolved at once - since I have no more eager [wish] than to show Your p in everything how much I [strive] to answer to your wishes - also

to resolve to send such back into their hands forthwith, be it even at the greatest sacrifice. And since I still had to draw from the moneys deposited for the war-treasury roughly as much as the sum instructed to Mr. Eys. amounted to, I have accordingly, upon receipt of the letter from you, requested Mr. [uncertain: Ulli.] Koppe in writing to pay Mr. Eys. without delay the sum owing, the 2500 Rthl, and in return to take back the Alligl. from Your (which Herr 9. M. A. holds in safekeeping), and to deliver the same to the same. Now since Mr. Assessor Koppe is back again - as letters from Heidelburg, where he passed through, inform me - I therefore consider my commission to him as executed and Your wish in this matter as fulfilled. From the foregoing more exact narration of the history you will only deign to satisfy yourself that I have absolutely done nothing in this affair which does not bear the stamp of the greatest high respect and friendship for the same, [continued]

bears, and that therefore the expressions contained, as the same say, in the [uncertain: Mayndl.] letter do not proceed from me, nor was it in any way my intention to represent the matter from the side apprehended by Your p, since I shall rather always be most highly grateful to you for that which the same have done for me (as in friendship). To this assurance you will now be unable to withhold the fullest credence, when I have the honour to report to you here that I am sending you the amount of 3000 Rthl Courant demanded in your last letter of the 25th of last month. Your etc. may believe that I thereby deprive myself almost of my last moneys, in order to answer to your wishes, and truly it required nothing less than the strength of my attachment to you to resolve upon this step also. I now beg the same to bring the whole affair to a complete conclusion, and to convey to me the earliest report upon it. The

The enclosed Rthlr to - Amelang, deign to have forwarded to the authority, even though I may indeed expect that the retradition of the Alligl. will already have taken place by then. From Your last esteemed letter I should almost conjecture that the same do not stand on the best terms with Minister Mr. v. Stein. I must confess frankly to the same that this would pain me greatly, since I believe that this gentleman is one of those who must in any event be spared. I much wished that on your journey to Vienna you might give me the pleasure of visiting me here in person. This would be quite extraordinarily welcome to me, inasmuch as it is not possible to settle in writing everything upon which I should very gladly hear your counsel and upon which I should like to have information from you. Gladly would I have resolved to send a confidant to you for that purpose, but I am held back solely by

the thought that Your p might perhaps not gladly say to anyone else than to myself all that would be worth my knowing. I know therefore of no other means than an [uncertain: expubesucht] from [uncertain: Emp.] here as far as -, which would cause no too great a detour, since you are travelling by way of Dresden in any case; and I therefore most urgently request the same, wherever at all possible, to give me this pleasure. Should you think it advisable to say something of it to Mr. Assessor Koppe, then I beg for it. In respect of the money business I am not idle here, only that before the lapse of 8-14 days I [can] say nothing further upon it, because various papers are still wanting to that end, which I [expect] daily. I beg only for this, that care be taken that the cession of the mortgage take place at once, should such be required, so that the business find no [impediment] thereby. My court factor here I have ordered to report himself in [illegible]; on which account I the more wish that the same might await his arrival at Berlin, since I believe he would be of use for a money business very much to be wished by me, [uncertain: quarterly]. What I received yesterday in respect of the Wildegans, I send Your here in copy, with the request that you instruct me what may be to be done in the matter, and also, in order to give the occasion, so that Your might in this initiate the step that seems serviceable to you. With the same request you receive one here, which was a proposal made by [uncertain: Jeg.] concerning a [uncertain: Takt], and I very much request the same to let me have your opinion and counsel upon it with all speed. Your Right Honourable's [uncertain: Öh] 13 March 1808 To Your Right Honourable the Councillor of War and Forests v. Fr.

summary_en: Defends himself at length against the suspicion, raised in Triebenfeld's letter of the 20th, of unfriendly conduct, and narrates the history of the Berlin creditor Eysenhardt (Eysach), settled in January 1807 through the Privy Councillor Major: the 6000 Rthlr instruction from Stettinius was ceded to him against 2500 Rthlr, the remaining 3500 Rthlr being lost when payment was suspended; Assessor Koppe has been instructed to pay Eysenhardt and retrieve the Alligl. Encloses 3000 Rthlr Courant, remarks on relations with Minister v. Stein, presses for a personal visit en route to Vienna via Dresden, and asks advice on the Wildegans matter.
summary_de: Rechtfertigung gegen den Verdacht unfreundlichen Verhaltens: Ausführliche Darstellung der Anweisung über 6000 Rthl von Stettinius, die im Januar 1807 zur Abfindung des Berliner Gläubigers Eysenhardt (1500 bzw. 2500 Rthl) unter Vermittlung des Geheimen Raths Meyer cedirt wurde, sowie der in Breslau veranlassten Zahlungssperre; Assessor Koppe ist angewiesen, Eysenhardt die 2500 Rthl zu zahlen und das Alligl. zurückzunehmen. Übersendung von 3000 Rthl Courant; Beilage für Amelang; Bemerkung zum Verhältnis zu Minister v. Stein; Bitte um persönlichen Besuch auf der Reise nach Wien über Dresden; Anfragen zur Sache Wildegans.
